summary: Describes how RSVP-TE traffic engineering can be supported in BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPNs, where a provider edge node serves multiple customers in different VPNs. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: Many businesses share one big network, each with a private lane. This explains how to reserve special fast lanes for one business without mixing it up with others.

questions: can rsvp-te be used in l3vpn
how to support traffic engineering across vpns
what are the new rsvp-te objects for vpns
how does rsvp-te identify the vpn in l3vpn
subtitle: Extensions to RSVP-TE for quality-of-service tunnels within BGP/MPLS Layer 3 virtual private networks.

tldr.problem: Service providers use BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPNs to offer private connectivity to multiple customers over a shared backbone. When a provider edge router handles multiple VPNs with traffic engineering, RSVP-TE control messages arrive stripped of their VPN labels, and the PE cannot tell which VPN each message belongs to.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6882 defines new RSVP-TE object types that embed VPN identifiers directly in the protocol messages, allowing provider edge routers to identify and correctly route RSVP-TE control messages for multiple VPNs without relying on labels.
tldr.outcome: This experimental approach enables service providers to offer traffic-engineered paths within L3VPNs without requiring complex label-aware RSVP processing at PE routers, providing an alternative to the label-based approach in RFC 4364.

today: RFC 6882 is Experimental and has not been obsoleted. It provides an alternative experimental approach to supporting RSVP-TE in L3VPNs by embedding VPN identifiers in RSVP-TE messages, as opposed to the label-based approach of RFC 4364. This specification remains available for implementation and evaluation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6882 addresses a problem in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs where multiple customer sites need traffic-engineered paths. BGP/MPLS VPNs (defined in RFC 4364) allow service providers to offer VPN connectivity using provider edge (PE) routers that manage multiple customer VPNs. The fundamental issue is that when RSVP-TE control messages (Path and Resv messages) arrive at a PE from another PE, they have been processed by RSVP-TE and lose the VPN label context that identified which VPN the message belonged to.

RFC 4364 describes a label-based approach where VPNs are identified by labels during transport, and PE routers process RSVP messages within the appropriate VPN Routing and Forwarding (VRF) context. However, this approach requires PE routers to process RSVP messages in a VPN-aware manner, which is not straightforward in all implementations. RFC 6882 proposes an alternative experimental approach: embedding the VPN identifier directly in the RSVP-TE protocol message, so the PE can identify the VPN without relying on label context.
sections.eli5: Imagine two telephone companies sharing one backbone network, but each with their own private customer line. When a service request comes in, how does the system know which company it's for? This RFC puts the company name in the message itself.

sections.title: The VPN and RSVP-TE Challenge
sections.content:
Consider a network with two VPNs served by provider edge routers PE1 and PE2. Customer sites CE1 and CE2 belong to VPN1, and customer sites CE3 and CE4 belong to VPN2. Both pairs want to establish MPLS traffic-engineered paths using RSVP-TE. CE1 sends a Path message to PE1 destined for CE2. PE1 can identify the VPN from the incoming interface, looks up the remote PE (PE2) through routing, and forwards the Path message.

The problem arises at PE2. The incoming message carries an MPLS label that identifies the VPN, but once the message is handed to the RSVP-TE component for processing, that label context is lost. PE2 sees two Path messages (one from VPN1 and one from VPN2) but cannot distinguish which is which to forward them to the correct customer edge router. RFC 6882 solves this by defining new RSVP object types that carry VPN addresses directly in the RSVP message.
sections.eli5: The post office receives packages labeled for both companies, but once they're sorted by the routing system, the labels come off. The solution is to write the company name inside the package itself.

sections.title: New RSVP-TE Objects for VPNs
sections.content:
The RFC defines new object types for SESSION, SENDER_TEMPLATE, and FILTER_SPEC, with IPv4 and IPv6 variants designated as LSP_TUNNEL_VPN-IPv4 and LSP_TUNNEL_VPN-IPv6. These objects are identical to the standard RSVP-TE objects, except the address fields contain VPN-IPv4 or VPN-IPv6 addresses, which include a Route Distinguisher (RD) prefix. The RD is a 12-byte value assigned by each provider to uniquely identify EID-to-RLOC mappings within that provider's domain.

For example, the LSP_TUNNEL_VPN-IPv4 SESSION object contains a 12-byte VPN-IPv4 tunnel endpoint address, a 2-byte Tunnel ID, and a 4-byte Extended Tunnel ID. Similarly, the SENDER_TEMPLATE object contains a VPN-IPv4 tunnel sender address and an LSP ID. The RFC also defines VPN-IPv4 and VPN-IPv6 RSVP_HOP objects analogous to those in RFC 6016. These objects are only used in messages between PEs within the provider backbone; messages sent outside the backbone use standard objects.
sections.eli5: Instead of using a label that gets stripped off, the message itself says 'For Company A' before it even leaves the backbone.

sections.title: Path and Resv Message Processing
sections.content:
When an ingress PE (PE1) receives a Path message from a customer edge router, it identifies the VPN from the incoming interface and determines the egress PE (PE2) by routing. The PE then constructs a new Path message replacing the standard SESSION and SENDER_TEMPLATE objects with VPN variants that include the Route Distinguisher along with the endpoint addresses. This modified Path message is sent directly to the egress PE.

At the egress PE, the VPN-IPv4 address is decoded to extract the RD and IP address, allowing the PE to identify the correct VRF context. The PE stores the entire incoming message and determines which customer edge router this belongs to. It then creates a new Path message with standard (non-VPN) objects and sends it toward the destination CE router with the IP Router Alert option. When the Resv message returns from the destination, the egress PE applies the reverse transformation, replacing standard objects with VPN variants and sending the message back to the ingress PE. The ingress PE decodes the VPN objects and forwards the message to the originating CE.
sections.eli5: When the package comes in, the PE1 reads 'Company A' and adds a special VPN label to the message before sending it to PE2. PE2 reads the VPN address inside the message to know it's Company A, then strips the label and sends a regular message to the customer. On the way back, it puts the VPN address in again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that general RSVP-TE security issues are covered in RFC 3209, and VPN-specific considerations are in RFC 4364, with broader MPLS security covered in RFC 5920. To secure RSVP control messages between PEs, the RFC recommends using RSVP Authentication as defined in RFC 2747 and updated by RFC 3097. For BGP messages used in VPN routing, TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) as specified in RFC 5925 MAY be used.

The embedding of VPN identifiers in RSVP messages does not itself introduce new security threats beyond those already present in the label-based approach. However, implementers must ensure that RSVP messages are only accepted from authorized sources and that the VPN context is correctly validated to prevent unauthorized PE-to-PE communication or traffic leakage between VPNs.
sections.eli5: The security of this approach relies on the same mechanisms as regular RSVP and VPNs—making sure that messages come from trusted sources and that the VPN context is correctly validated.
